text: You've now met linear models, decision trees, and forests. Two more classic algorithms round out the toolbox, and both think about the problem in a completely different way. k-nearest neighbors predicts by looking at similar examples. Naive Bayes predicts by multiplying probabilities. Neither is usually the final model in a serious project, but both make excellent fast baselines.

k-NN has almost no training step — it simply memorizes the training data. To predict for a new row, it finds the k training rows closest to it and lets them vote. If k is 5 and four of the five nearest customers churned, the prediction is churn. Closest means smallest distance, usually Euclidean, computed across every feature — and that single fact has a big consequence.

Using a seeded dataset with one feature multiplied by 1000, to mimic income sitting beside a rating score: fitting k-NN with k equals 5 on the raw, unscaled features scores just 0.453 — no better than a coin flip. The huge-scale feature completely drowns out everything else in the distance calculation.

Putting StandardScaler inside a pipeline before the same k-NN changes everything — the score jumps to 0.9. Same algorithm, same data, same k. Only the scale changed. Keeping the scaler inside the pipeline also protects against the data leakage you learned about earlier in this chapter.

Small k means a jagged, flexible boundary that chases noise. Large k means a smooth, blunt boundary that ignores local detail. On this scaled data, k of 1 scores a perfect 1.0 on training but only 0.9 on test — a classic overfit gap. k of 15 scores 0.913 on training and 0.927 on test, a much smaller, healthier gap.

Naive Bayes applies Bayes' rule directly — the probability of a class given the features is proportional to the prior probability of the class times the probability of seeing those features within that class. The naive part is assuming features are independent of each other given the class — rarely true, but the shortcut makes the math simple and training nearly instant.

GaussianNB scores 0.913 on the same test set, and predict_proba returns a probability for each class per row — for example, 0.131 and 0.869 for the first test row. scikit-learn also offers MultinomialNB for counts like word frequencies, which is why naive Bayes is a long-standing favorite for spam filtering and text classification.

When to reach for each: k-NN for small to medium datasets with few features and meaningful distances, though it's slow at prediction time on large data since it compares against every stored row. Naive Bayes is very fast, works with little data, and gives probabilities — a strong baseline for text.

To recap: scale your features and tune k for k-NN; naive Bayes multiplies class probabilities under an independence assumption. That completes our tour of trees and ensembles. Next, we leave supervised learning behind and start finding structure in data with no labels at all: clustering.
